walkthroughs.body_html:
Hazardous Environments — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Hazardous Environments brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Hazardous Environments.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Maghreb
Cape
Horn of Africa

options: 100mm
250mm
500mm

mcqs.q: Why does plastic accumulate in ocean gyres?
options: Plastic accumulates in gyres because the water there is denser.
The 'Great Pacific Garbage Patch' is a solid floating island of plastic you can walk on.
A spit is a small island just off the coast.

Gyres are large rotating ocean currents driven by wind and Coriolis effect; floating debris is carried in but the rotation traps it in the centre, where currents are weak, concentrating plastic over decades.
Continental crust subducts because it is thicker and heavier.
A spit is a small island just off the coast.
Longshore drift carries sediment past a change in coastline direction (e.g. river mouth); deposition continues into deeper water, building a curved depositional landform with a hook.
A spit forms where the river deposits its sediment at the coast.

mcqs.q: Why does oceanic crust subduct beneath continental crust?
options: Oceanic crust is denser (basaltic) than continental crust (granitic), so when they collide the denser oceanic plate sinks into the mantle, forming a trench and volcanic arc.
Continental crust subducts because it is thicker and heavier.
Oceanic crust subducts because the ocean pushes it down with its weight.
A spit is a small island just off the coast.
